content: A drug for high blood pressure could inspire future treatments for people with normal readings, thanks to an unexpected effect on the body’s energy-burning fat. Losartan already helps people control high blood pressure. New research suggests it could have a second use in activating brown fat, a tissue that burns energy to produce heat and is linked to better cardiovascular health. With a well-known safety profile, the drug could offer a practical way to investigate whether stimulating this tissue can bring health benefits to patients. That possibility emerged from medical records and PET/CT scans of more than 100,000 patients at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center (MSKCC). Researchers noticed that patients taking angiotensin receptor blockers, or ARBs, a class of blood pressure medications that includes losartan, were more likely to have brown fat detected on their scans. The study, published in Nature , brought together researchers in Rockefeller University’s Laboratory of Molecular Metabolism, led by Paul Cohen, and MSKCC researchers Heiko Schöder and Daniel Lafontaine. To understand what might explain the medication link, they worked backward from the patient observations to experiments in the lab. Cohen’s team has often used this approach, known as reverse translation, to investigate how brown fat works. When the researchers tested losartan in cultured brown fat cells, the drug directly increased their metabolic activity. It did so through molecular interactions distinct from those responsible for lowering blood pressure. “The fact that its different effects are mediated by different molecular pathways is advantageous, since it means we could potentially isolate them in future therapies,” says first author Nicolás Gómez-Banoy, an endocrinologist and instructor in clinical investigation in Cohen’s lab. “That way you would be able to stimulate brown fat in people with normal blood pressure.” Healthy mice treated with losartan also used more energy, consumed more oxygen, and produced more carbon dioxide, all while maintaining a steady body weight. These experiments support exploring a new use for the drug, although they do not establish that giving losartan to people to stimulate brown fat would improve their health. The human findings give researchers several connections to investigate. Alongside its links to cardiovascular health, brown fat was associated with lower rates of anxiety and depression, a connection to psychiatric health reported for the first time in this study. “We know that metabolically healthy people tend to have lower incidence of psychiatric diseases, so it could be that having brown fat makes you more metabolically healthy, and this correlates with fewer psychiatric issues,” says Gómez-Banoy. The analysis also linked SSRIs, medications commonly prescribed for depression, to reduced brown fat activity. How these observations fit together remains an open question, including whether brown fat itself contributes to the differences in mental health. Earlier work had focused more narrowly on the heart and metabolism. In 2021 , Cohen’s lab examined roughly 50,000 MSKCC patients and found that those with more brown fat had significantly lower odds of cardiometabolic diseases, including coronary artery disease and type 2 diabetes. “We only looked for a few diagnostic codes in that study, mainly focusing on cardiovascular disease since that’s what this tissue has historically been associated with,” says Cohen. “The scope of this new analysis is far more expansive. We doubled our number of patients and considered more than 500 codes, which allowed us to unearth many new insights.” The current study also looked beyond whether brown fat appeared on a scan to examine where it was active. The patients had undergone PET/CT scans as part of their cancer surveillance. Focusing on scans that detected brown adipose tissue, or BAT, Gómez-Banoy applied a machine learning tool developed by colleagues at MSKCC to measure its total activity in each patient and its activity in six anatomical regions. These included the neck, armpits, and areas surrounding the heart and kidneys. Measuring those regions separately revealed that the relationship with disease varied depending on where the brown fat was located. The researchers also compared brown fat with indicators of blood sugar regulation, blood fats, heart function, and inflammation. “For example, the axillary, or armpit, area was linked to a decreased risk of high blood pressure compared to other regions,” he says. “But overall, patients with brown fat have better glycemic parameters, lipid profiles, and echocardiographic indices, as well as lower inflammatory markers.” Brown fat was also associated with higher rates of osteoporosis and skin diseases, raising questions about possible downsides. Further research could investigate those associations, examine the genetics of people with high BAT levels, and explore the connection to anxiety and depression. “There were plenty of other medications associated with brown fat activity in our large cohort,” Cohen notes. “This is just a start.” Reference: “Artificial intelligence-enabled clinical phenotyping of human brown fat” by Nicolás Gómez-Banoy, Jorge A. Barrero, Luiza Rachel Pinheiro de Carvalho, Caroline S. content: The promise of an experimental treatment for C. difficile gut infections lies partly in the bacteria it leaves alive, according to early laboratory and mouse research. Broad-spectrum antibiotics can disrupt the gut’s microbial community, allowing a bacterium already living there to multiply unchecked. Clostridioides difficile , or C. difficile , is naturally present in the intestines of many people and usually causes no symptoms when its numbers remain low. When it proliferates, however, its toxins can trigger acute intestinal inflammation that may become chronic and can sometimes be life-threatening. These infections, known as CDI, are among the leading causes of antibiotic-associated diarrhea and have high relapse rates. After multiple relapses, patients are often treated with fecal microbiota transfer, commonly called a stool transplant. The procedure is complex and unpleasant for many patients, creating a need for treatments that control the infection while limiting further disruption of the gut’s microbes. A team led by Professor Rolf Müller, department head and scientific director at HIPS, has identified a drug candidate that specifically kills C. difficile while sparing much of the gut microbiome. HIPS is a site of the Helmholtz Centre for Infection Research (HZI) in collaboration with Saarland University. The candidate, argyrin B, belongs to a group of natural compounds identified in soil-dwelling myxobacteria. These bacteria use such compounds to hunt other microorganisms and exploit them as food. “We were able to show that the natural compound argyrin B is highly effective against CDI: both in laboratory experiments and in a mouse model of the infection, where it significantly reduces the bacterial load,” says Dr. Jennifer Herrmann, a senior scientist in the “Microbial Natural Products” department at HIPS. For argyrins to become medicines, researchers must evaluate both their effectiveness and their pharmaceutical properties, including how they move through the body. When the team gave argyrin B to mice by mouth, very little entered the bloodstream. Instead, it remained largely in the large intestine, where the treatment is needed. Keeping the compound concentrated there could help limit unwanted effects elsewhere in the body, suggesting a potentially well-tolerated approach to treating CDI. Herrmann also describes how the compound acts against the bacterium and what its selectivity could mean for recovery. “An antibacterial target of the argyrins had previously been identified and characterized in the notorious hospital-acquired pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa . Now we have been able to show that argyrin B also acts on this target in C. difficile and exhibits particularly high efficacy in doing so. In contrast, the argyrins have virtually no effect on the beneficial microorganisms in our digestive tract. The gut microbiome could therefore be spared during treatment with argyrin and restored to a healthy state more quickly.” An argyrin-based treatment could reduce the risk of further microbiome disruption, infections, and relapses that would otherwise require a stool transplant. In follow-up studies, the researchers plan to determine the dose of argyrin B that achieves maximum efficacy and use appropriate models to test its effectiveness against recurrent infections. Reference: “Argyrin B exhibits potent therapeutic efficacy in a Clostridioides difficile-infection mouse model while preserving microbiota functionality” by Sari Rasheed, Katrin Ehrhardt, Ahmed Mohamed Mostafa Abdrabou, Alexander Mellmann, Anna Lechleiter, Domen Pogorevc, Sabryna Junker, Lutz von Müller, Marius Vital, Jennifer Herrmann, Guntram A.
